prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Tonight I light the candles of my eyes in the lee And swing down this branch full of red leaves. Yellow moon, skull and spine of the hare, Arrow me to town on the neck of the air. I hear the undertaker make love in the heather; The candy maker, poor fellow, is under the weather. Skunk, moose, raccoon, they go to the doors in threes With a torch in their hands or pleas: "O, please . . ." Baruch Spinoza and the butcher are drunk: One is the tail and one is the trunk Of a beast who dances in circles for beer And doesn't think twice to learn how to steer. Our clock is blind, our clock is dumb. Its hands are broken, its fingers numb. No time for the martyr of our fair town Who wasn't a witch because she could drown. Now the dogs of the cemetery are starting to bark At the vision of her, bobbing up through the dark. When she opens her mouth to gasp for air, A moth flies out and lands in her hair. The apples are thumping, winter is coming. The lips of the pumpkin soon will be humming. By the caw of the crow on the first of the year, Something will die, something appear.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Tonight, And, Yellow

outputs.L1:
Tonight, I light the candles of my eyes in the lee,  
And swing down this branch, full of red leaves.  
Yellow moon, skull and spine of the hare,  
Arrow me to town on the neck of the air.  

I hear the undertaker make love in the heather;  
The candy maker, poor fellow, is under the weather.  
Skunk, moose, and raccoon go to the doors in threes,  
With torches in their hands, or pleas: “O, please . . .”  

Baruch Spinoza and the butcher are drunk:  
One is the tail, and one is the trunk  
Of a beast that dances in circles for beer,  
And does not think twice to learn how to steer.  

Our clock is blind; our clock is dumb.  
Its hands are broken, its fingers numb.  
No time for the martyr of our fair town,  
Who was not a witch because she could drown.  

Now the dogs of the cemetery are starting to bark  
At the vision of her, bobbing up through the dark.  
When she opens her mouth to gasp for air,  
A moth flies out and lands in her hair.  

The apples are thumping; winter is coming.  
The lips of the pumpkin soon will be humming.  
By the caw of the crow on the first of the year,  
Something will die; something will appear.

outputs.L3:
The poem presents a surreal nocturnal scene filled with vivid and unsettling images. Candles, red leaves, the moon, and mysterious movements toward town combine to create an atmosphere that feels both dreamlike and ominous. The night is not calm or ordinary; instead, it seems alive with strange signs and symbolic gestures. The imagery suggests a world caught between waking and dreaming, where familiar objects and places take on a magical or threatening quality.

Animals and townspeople appear in uncanny pairings, adding to the poem’s sense of disorder. Their actions seem ritualistic, drunken, or irrational, as if the normal rules of behavior have been suspended. These unusual combinations create the impression of a community participating, consciously or unconsciously, in some strange ceremony. The result is a mood of confusion and instability, where human and animal worlds blur together and the town becomes part of a larger, mysterious pattern.

Time itself is portrayed as broken and useless. The image of a blind, dumb clock with numb fingers suggests that time can no longer guide, measure, or explain what is happening. A clock is normally associated with order, routine, and clarity, but here it has lost its senses and its power. It cannot see, speak, or move properly. This image reinforces the poem’s dreamlike atmosphere, suggesting that the events take place outside ordinary time or in a moment when time has become meaningless.

The poem also strongly evokes death and haunting. References to an undertaker, a cemetery, barking dogs, and a drowned woman rising from the dark introduce a ghostly and threatening presence. These images suggest that the boundary between the living and the dead has become unstable. The drowned woman’s emergence from darkness is especially haunting, as it implies that the past, the buried, or the forgotten is returning. The poem’s night world is therefore not only strange but also filled with reminders of mortality and unresolved grief.

Finally, the poem suggests seasonal change and the presence of omens. The red leaves and other signs of transition point toward autumn, decay, and the ending of one phase of life. Yet the poem does not present death as merely final. Instead, it hints at an approaching transformation in which something must die so that something new can appear. The unsettling images, broken time, and haunted atmosphere all contribute to a sense of anticipation. The poem becomes a vision of change: dark, mysterious, and disturbing, but also charged with the possibility of renewal.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a surreal and ominous vision of a town caught on the threshold of change. Its setting feels unstable, as though the community exists between seasons, between waking and dreaming, and between the living world and a darker spiritual realm. Through grotesque imagery and strange, unsettling details, the poem transforms ordinary streets, houses, weather, and human figures into signs of decay, fear, and hidden meaning. The town is not described realistically; instead, it appears distorted by imagination, folklore, and nightmare. Familiar elements of communal life become mysterious and threatening, suggesting that beneath the surface of everyday existence lie guilt, death, memory, and ancient superstition.

The poem’s use of personification gives the natural world an eerie vitality. Seasons, objects, and landscapes seem to act with intention, as if the town itself were alive and aware of the changes taking place within it. This creates a dreamlike atmosphere in which boundaries collapse: the natural and supernatural mingle, the past intrudes upon the present, and the dead seem close to the living. Folkloric references deepen this effect, connecting the town’s experiences to older rituals, fears, and beliefs. The poem suggests that seasonal transition is not merely a change in weather, but a spiritual passage involving loss, judgment, and renewal.

At the same time, the poem does not present decay as purely destructive. Although its imagery is dark and grotesque, it also points toward transformation. Death, guilt, and corruption are shown as part of a larger cycle in which endings make renewal possible. The town becomes a symbolic space where time folds in on itself and where communal history, natural rhythms, and spiritual anxiety all converge. In this world, nothing remains fixed: bodies, seasons, memories, and beliefs are constantly shifting. The poem ultimately suggests that decay and transformation are unavoidable forces, shaping both human communities and the natural world.

Tonight, the city feels softer than usual. Streetlights glow in a warm yellow haze, painting the sidewalks with gentle pools of light. And as the evening settles in, every sound seems quieter—the distant traffic, the whispering trees, the slow footsteps of people heading home.

There is something peaceful about moments like this. The sky grows darker, the windows shine brighter, and the world seems to pause for just a little while. Tonight is not loud or hurried. It is calm, golden, and full of quiet possibility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal Halloween poem with witches, animals, pumpkins, cemeteries, and an ominous nursery-rhyme rhythm.
counterfactuals.output:
Three black kittens in a row,  
Blink where moonlit mushrooms grow.  
One says hush and one says soon,  
One eats shadows with a spoon.  

Witches stitch the midnight sky,  
With bat-wing thread and spider’s eye.  
Round the pumpkin, pale and wide,  
Grinning with a ghost inside.  

In the cemetery, softly, softly,  
Bones play fiddles, off-key, off-key.  
Rabbits drum on coffin lids,  
Foxes dance like wicked kids.  

“Come away,” the scarecrows sing,  
“Wear a worm for a wedding ring.  
Step by step and toe by toe,  
Down where the crooked lilies grow.”  

Owls pour tea from silver skulls,  
Mice ride beetles, dressed as gulls.  
Witches laugh and clap and croon:  
“Rock the graveyard, rock the moon.”  

Pumpkin eyes begin to weep,  
Orange dreams too bright to keep.  
All the stones lean close to hear  
Someone whisper, “Night is near.”  

Hush now, hush now, don’t look back,  
Hooves go clatter on the track.  
If you wake before the dawn,  
Count your teeth—one may be gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, whimsical poem in the style of mid-century confessional poetry, full of strange autumn imagery and folklore.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep a little October under my tongue,  
bitter as walnut skin, black as a match head.  
At night it clicks its bones and sings  
of foxfire, of kettles left cold,  
of mothers who bury their mirrors in the yard.

The orchard wears its bruises openly.  
Apples fall with the dull consent of hearts,  
each one a small red planet gone wrong.  
I gather them in my apron  
like evidence, like sins,  
while crows stitch the sky shut overhead.

There is a witch in the hedgerow  
combing burrs from her hair with a fish spine.  
She knows my name from before I had one.  
She says the dead are only shy this season,  
hiding in gourds, in cellar dust,  
in the soft mouths of mushrooms.

How domestic it all becomes—  
the moon rinsed white in a tin basin,  
the stove coughing up blue tongues,  
my grief folded neat beside the linens.  
I have been a good daughter to disaster.  
I have set a place for it every evening.

Outside, the pumpkins glow like severed thoughts.  
The wind goes door to door,  
begging in its ragged coat.  
Somewhere a black dog crosses a bridge  
and turns into my father’s shadow.  
Somewhere a child is told not to follow the lights  
dancing over the marsh.

But I follow.  
Of course I follow.

My boots fill with leaves and cold water.  
The reeds whisper psalms in a language of teeth.  
The will-o’-the-wisps bob ahead,  
little lanterns of fever,  
little promises with no houses inside them.

By dawn I am back in my own kitchen,  
mud on my hem, ash in my hair,  
a crescent moon tucked under one fingernail.  
The kettle shrieks like a thing being born.  
The windows fog with ghost-breath.

And I, that old autumn animal,  
that girl-shaped superstition,  
lift the cup to my lips  
and drink the dark down,  
sweetened with cloves,  
warm as a curse.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a gothic autumn poem that mentions Spinoza, a butcher, an undertaker, a candy maker, and animals going door to door.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath October’s iron moon, the withered orchards sighed,  
And leaves like rusted funeral coins went skittering far and wide.  
Old Spinoza’s name was carved upon the chapel stone,  
Where ravens read philosophy to bones left all alone.  

The butcher shut his crimson shop and barred the dripping door,  
While shadows licked the cobblestones and asked him for one more.  
The undertaker, tall and pale, with gloves of ashen lace,  
Measured the wind for coffins in the graveyard’s hollow space.  

A candy maker stirred black sweets in cauldrons copper-bright,  
Spun sugar webs for ghostly tongues that wandered through the night.  
And down the lane came animals, in masks of straw and thread—  
Fox, crow, and cat went door to door to beg among the dead.  

They tapped with claws on windowpanes, they whispered, “Treat or bone,”  
As autumn closed its velvet fist around each haunted home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a creepy lyrical poem for Halloween night, with red leaves, a yellow moon, broken clocks, drowned witches, crows, pumpkins, and winter approaching.
counterfactuals.output:
On Halloween, the red leaves crawl  
like little flames along the wall,  
and in the fields the pumpkins grin  
with candle-teeth and rot within.  

A yellow moon, so thin, so old,  
hangs in the sky like tarnished gold;  
it watches roads where no feet go,  
where black crows stitch the wind with woe.  

The broken clocks in the empty hall  
tick backward once, then not at all;  
their hands point down, their faces cracked,  
as if the dead are coming back.  

Beneath the bridge, where river reeds  
are tangled thick with moonlit weeds,  
the drowned witches lift their hair  
and whisper spells into the air.  

They call the frost from root and bone,  
they call the dark to claim its own;  
the crows all cry, the shutters sigh,  
the yellow moon climbs cold and high.  

And far beyond the pumpkin light,  
winter is walking through the night—  
with silver breath and silent feet,  
to lay white sheets on every street.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming, dreamlike poem about a haunted town on Halloween, mixing absurd humor with eerie supernatural images.
counterfactuals.output:
On Halloween, when clocks forgot  
And sneezed out sparks of blue,  
A haunted town called Crumplepot  
Awoke at half-past two.  

The moon wore socks, the stars wore hats,  
The wind began to croon,  
While ghostly mice in velvet spats  
Waltzed backward through a spoon.  

The pumpkins grinned with candle tongues,  
They whispered, “Run away!”  
Then coughed up bats with tiny lungs  
Who sang in opera “Boo-lay!”  

The church bell rang though no church stood,  
The steeple drifted by,  
A skeleton in a yellow hood  
Sold pies to passersby.  

“Fresh doom!” he cried. “A slice of fright!  
Two screams for just a dime!”  
A werewolf paid and, with delight,  
Ate crust and howled in rhyme.  

Down Fogbone Lane, the houses leaned  
Like secrets dressed in brick,  
Their windows blinked, their chimneys preened,  
Their shadows ran off sick.  

A phantom mayor made of smoke  
Declared, “No feet allowed!”  
Then tripped upon his own bad joke  
And vanished in a cloud.  

The graveyard yawned. The headstones danced  
A jig with worms in wigs,  
While moonlit coffins flipped and pranced  
Like nervous wooden pigs.  

I met a witch with teacup eyes  
Who stirred the night with string,  
She baked a cake of moths and lies  
And fed it to the king.  

The king, a frog with seven crowns,  
Proclaimed the soup was thin,  
Then swallowed three suspicious nouns  
And burped a violin.  

Yet under all the nonsense bright,  
A colder music grew—  
The alleys stretched into the night,  
The fog began to chew.  

Tall spirits climbed the crooked air  
With lanterns in their teeth,  
And something smiled behind the stair  
That had no underneath.  

The town went hush. The candles bent.  
The black cats formed a choir.  
A door appeared where none was meant,  
All trimmed with greenish fire.  

It creaked and spoke my secret name,  
Then giggled like a shoe;  
I turned to flee the misty flame—  
The street fled with me too.  

So if you hear at half-past dead  
A pumpkin softly sneeze,  
Don’t follow where the moon is led  
By ghosts on bumblebees.  

For Crumplepot, on Halloween,  
Still dreams beneath the ground,  
Where silly shadows, sharp and green,  
Laugh low without a sound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
